title: Jeremiah 7:29–34
context: The LORD calls Jerusalem, addressed in the feminine as a mourning daughter, to cut off her hair and lament on the bare heights, for he has rejected “the generation of his wrath” (7:29). He then names the abominations set in his house and the high places of Topheth in the valley of the son of Hinnom, where the people burned their sons and daughters in the fire, “which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind” (7:30–31). The same practice is named in 19:5 and 32:35, and Josiah’s defiling of Topheth is reported in 2 Kings 23:10. The LORD announces that the place will be called “The valley of Slaughter,” that the dead will lie unburied, and that the voices of joy and of bride and bridegroom will cease (7:32–34). This page reports these words soberly and does not expand on the practice beyond what the text states. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: God condemns the sacrifice of children without reserve, and his judgment answers real and grievous wrong.

verses.text: Cut off your hair, and throw it away, and take up a lamentation on the bare heights; for the LORD has rejected and forsaken the generation of his wrath.
verses.arminianNotes: “Cut off your hair, and throw it away, and take up a lamentation.” Arminian readers note the call to mourning, addressed to Jerusalem as a grieving daughter. The appropriate response to judgment is lament.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the cutting of hair as a sign of grief and the call to lament as fitting. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as summoning the people to mourn, and both read “the generation of his wrath” as describing a generation under judgment.

verses.text: “For the children of Judah have done that which is evil in my sight,” says the LORD. “They have set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to defile it.
verses.arminianNotes: “They have set their abominations in the house which is called by my name.” Arminian readers note that idolatry has entered the temple itself, defiling the very place the people trusted for security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the defilement of God’s house as a grievous offense against his holiness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting the temple sermon’s warning (7:4) with the people’s actual conduct in the house of God.

verses.text: They have built the high places of Topheth, which is in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.
verses.arminianNotes: They burned their sons and daughters at Topheth, “which I didn’t command, nor did it come into my mind.” Arminian readers stress God’s total rejection of the practice. It was entirely contrary to his will (compare 19:5 and 32:35).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear an absolute condemnation of child sacrifice and note that the LORD disowns it entirely. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with sobriety and grief, affirming that God never commanded such evil and condemns it without reserve.

verses.text: Therefore behold, the days come”, says the LORD, “that it will no more be called ‘Topheth’ or ‘The valley of the son of Hinnom’, but ‘The valley of Slaughter’; for they will bury in Topheth until there is no place to bury.
verses.arminianNotes: Topheth will be called “The valley of Slaughter,” and they will bury there until no room is left. Arminian readers note the grim reversal: the place of these deaths becomes a place of burial for the people themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment answering the crime at the very place where it was committed. Shared ground: both traditions report the verse soberly, without expanding on its details, and see it as God’s just response to the evil named in 7:31.

verses.text: The dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds of the sky, and for the animals of the earth. No one will frighten them away.
verses.arminianNotes: “The dead bodies of this people will be food for the birds.” Arminian readers note the horror of being left unburied in the ancient world. They report the image soberly as part of the announced judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as a covenant curse coming to pass. Shared ground: both traditions handle the verse with pastoral sobriety, neither softening nor dwelling on its details, and both see it as the consequence of persistent rebellion.

verses.text: Then I will cause to cease from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride; for the land will become a waste.”
verses.arminianNotes: The voices of mirth, gladness, bridegroom, and bride will cease. Arminian readers note the loss of ordinary joy. Judgment touches not only temple and city but weddings and celebrations, the daily gladness of life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the silencing of joy as a sign of the land’s desolation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with grief and note that the same phrase appears later in Jeremiah with the promise of restoration (compare 33:11).
